caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No — and the man who made it wanted you to know.

On October 16, 1869, two men digging a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, hit a ten-foot stone man. One reportedly said, "I declare, some old Indian has been buried here!" A tent went up. Newell charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes. Three to five hundred people came a day.

The figure was carved from a block of gypsum quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, in 1868 — the quarrymen were told it was for a Lincoln monument. It went to Chicago, where two sculptors shaped it behind hung quilts to muffle the noise. Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles gave it pores and age. It was modelled on its maker, George Hull, a tobacconist who had lost an argument at a revival meeting about the giants in Genesis 6:4.

Geologists arrived. Andrew D. White noticed nobody would dig a well there — there was already a good spring. Yale's Othniel C. Marsh saw fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum and called it "a most decided humbug." Some theologians defended it anyway.

Hull sold his interest for $23,000. P. T. Barnum, refused at $50,000, had a wax model made in secret and exhibited his own copy. Hull confessed on December 10, 1869. Both giants were ruled fakes in court on February 2, 1870.

What stays unsettled: whether the Chicago stonecutter who took the commission knew what he was making. The record does not say.

Images: the giant photographed by Bain News Service, 1910; an 1869 lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant"; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry, from the New York Public Library.
